My disdain for fat people is outward and loud. She hears it. But knowing how girls typically are (I'm not trying to be sexist, just going based on my experience over my lifetime), I know that can be a tricky line to balance, keeping them aware of what's OK and what isn't, and not fostering massive self-worth and self-confidence anxiety issues.

So how can I make sure that she knows how to stay healthy and fit, but not cause issues at the same time?
How can I teach my daughter to be healthy but not make her neurotic about it?

No kids here so I can only go by what I perceive is good parenting. My SIL/BIL have raised three very fit healthy young adults, all of whom are now in college.

The two main things I saw them do that guided my nieces and nephew to be humans are 1) set a good example by living well. SIL/BIL are runners and would encourage the kids to come along. They grew up thinking that exercise is as normal as brushing your teeth and wiping your ass. 2) From a very, very young age they would repeatedly ask the kids, "what will be the consequences of that decision?" The topic could be anything from sharing with siblings, to not doing homework, and of course, eating properly. The rest of us extended family picked up on this question and we would all regularly ask them that.

I get the impression they now ALWAYS ask themselves that question before making any decision. Currently, one niece is about to graduate college and embark on a career as a physical therapist, the nephew is on a full scholarship for baseball and is majoring in nutrition, and the youngest niece just started nursing school. All human. I'm so proud of them. They have made many good decisions so far.

Good luck, Dad!

I'm a stepmother to a 7-year-old boy who is living with two extremes. He loves working out with Daddy. When Daddy is doing pushups, he does pushups. He knows because of our gentle advice to him that eating the right things and sleeping enough will make him grow muscles. He likes feeling strong, and even though he might not always like some of the healthy things I cook, we impress upon him that it's important to try things and try them more than once because your tastes change over time. So he understands, on whatever level a boy his age can, that some day he may actually grow to like some of the healthy foods I feed him now that he doesn't like. Brussels sprouts are a good example. I didn't like them when I was younger and my mom didn't feed them to us anyway. I make them because I like them, and he knows there's a good chance that he'll like them when he grows up, and they're good for him now, so he'll eat them here and there. He loves bike rides, which he can't do with mommy because she doesn't have a bike(had to sell them because she's bankrupt and probably too fat to ride one anyway. Has arthritis in her knees too at 36). I don't think he's made the connection yet between her weight her and her lifestyle and certainly hasn't made the connection between her lifestyle and her finances. His dad and I have a healthy, active lifestyle and we have more money, so he can see the trickle-down effect of those things to him, where we can take him to the park and on bike rides and his mother can't. He gets grounded more at her house and gets into more trouble, whereas he rarely gets in trouble for anything here beyond minor talking back, which is rarely an issue. We try to impress upon him that he's allowed to disagree with us, but he still has to obey us and his teachers in the same way that my husband and I are allowed to disagree and discuss things with our bosses and senior colleagues but still have to submit to their leadership.

Basically, from my own experience with parenting to this point, having raised this boy now for 5-and-a-half years, I've come to see that you impress lessons upon your children both by your personal example and by teaching them in a very real way the consequences of certain actions. We don't say "Mommy does X or doesn't do X because she's fat/smokes/drinks too much," but it's a connection he'll make in time. It's better to show a positive way of being, and eventually when he's more aware of his surroundings due to increased maturity, hopefully he'll say, "I shouldn't eat too much of that because it will make me fat and sick," or "I shouldn't smoke because then I won't be able to go on these bike rides and swims and play soccer."

Your disdain for fat people, in my opinion, is fine. You know how they are at this age: They naturally feel the same as you do about fat people, or, indeed, anyone who is clearly "different." Children are merciless when it comes to that. As long as your daughter internalizes self-confidence in her abilities as she grows, I don't think you'll have a problem. What my dad did did not work in this regard. He shamed me when I didn't want to come on family bike rides, making me less likely to want to go and not realizing that I was dealing with pretty major depressive issues even as a child because I was different and didn't have a lot of friends. The better lesson that I took away and will apply to my own parenting will be to say to my stepson, and any future children, "Come on, come with us. I can see you're not feeling great, but we want to spend time with you and it will make you feel better to get out of the house and do something with us." That's how we've dealt with the issue so far, and my stepson largely responds very positively to it.
